newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco companies agree to $368.5 billion settlement.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco companies agree to $368.5 billion settlement.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Legal Correspondent
Tobacco companies agreed to pay $368.5 billion, admit that tobacco is addictive and accept extensive federal regulation over their products and their advertising as part of a landmark agreement.

In return, the companies, which have never before been forced to pay for tobacco-related illnesses, would be given immunity from any further punitive liability for deception, fraud or conspiracy that might have occurred in the past.

The agreement is by far the largest ever involving an industry and concludes two months of negotiations that grew from an innovative lawsuit filed by Mississippi's attorney general without the knowledge of his governor.

"We are here today to announce what ... we believe is the most historic public health achievement in history," Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore told a news conference. "We have reached agreement in principle with the tobacco industry."
Reading from a statement on behalf of the tobacco industry, Philip Morris Cos. Inc. Senior Vice President Steven Parrish said the industry disagreed with some elements of the proposed settlement.
"The proposal is a bitter pill because our companies have made concessions that were extremely difficult," he said.
"But on balance, this plan is preferable to a continuation of a decades-long controversy that has failed to produce a constructive outcome for anyone."
The agreement was announced at packed news conference in the nation's capital and was immediately hailed by President Bill Clinton, who said he would appoint a task force to review its terms.

"We must now carefully consider whether approving this proposed settlement will protect the public health," he said in a statement that named Donna Shalala, Health and Human Services secretary, and White House aide Bruce Reed in charge of the review.
Forty states have sued the industry to recoup Medicaid costs of treating sick smokers. Talks between the industry and the state attorneys general had been going on since early April.
In a statement of their own, the state attorneys general, the highest ranking legal officers in each of the individual states, said the tobacco industry would pay the $368.5 billion over 25 years.

The agreement requires that the industry curb the marketing of cigarettes to children and bans the sale of cigarettes from vending machines and self-service displays. The industry would be penalised unless tobacco use by children declines by specific targets.

"The Marlboro Man will be riding into the sunset on Joe Camel," Florida Attorney General Robert Butterworth said. "An industry that has never been regulated before is now the most regulated industry in America and that is the way it should be."
The agreement also calls for tobacco firms to make a statement acknowledging the dangers of tobacco.
"We wanted this industry to have to change the way they do business and we have done that," Moore said.
It was Moore who launched the nationwide blitz against the tobacco industry in May 1994 when he sued the major tobacco companies to recover the cost of treating tobacco-related illnesses.

Arizona Attorney General Grant Woods, who participated in the negotiations, said, "The tobacco companies are now going to put on the front of their packages ... the following statements: 'Cigarettes are addictive. Cigarettes cause fatal lung cancer. Cigarettes cause cancer. Smoking can kill you. Tobacco smoke can harm your children...'"

The agreement would recognise that the FDA has regulatory power over tobacco products, including the authority to reduce the levels of nicotine and eventually eliminate it, the statement said. Under the deal, the FDA would have the authority to ban nicotine after 12 years.
The agreement would enact into law current FDA rules to protect children from tobacco marketing.

It also would require FDA approval of all ingredients in tobacco products and standards for reducing harmful components, including nicotine. The proposed agreement mandates testing of ingredients and safety assessments, the statement said.

The agreement would require the tobacco industry to hand over to the FDA all research it conducts. It also would impose penalties for any violations that are 10 times those facing other companies regulated by the FDA, the attorneys general said.
